claims.claim: Kirner-Ludwig asserts that Martin himself lacks expert knowledge of the historical stages of English.
claims.quote: That is even true for George R. R. Martin himself.

claims.claim: The PNAS study states that A Song of Ice and Fire is presented from the personal perspectives of 24 point of view characters.
claims.quote: presented from the personal perspectives of 24 point of view (POV) characters

claims.claim: The PNAS study counts 14 of the point of view characters as major, defined as having eight or more chapters.
claims.quote: we consider 14 to be major: eight or more chapters

claims.claim: The PNAS study counts 343 chapters across the five published novels and identifies 2,007 characters in them.
claims.page: Results, 'Evolution of the Social Network Structure'

claims.claim: The PNAS study finds 1,806 of the identified characters interact with another character at least once.
claims.quote: of which 1,806 interact with another at least once
claims.page: Results, 'Evolution of the Social Network Structure'

claims.claim: The PNAS study finds the intervals between significant deaths measured in chapters are geometrically rather than power-law distributed, which it reads as measurable support for the deaths being unpredictable chapter by chapter.
claims.quote: it is geometric rather than power law

claims.feature: other: discourse order versus story order
claims.claim: The PNAS study reports that the order and pacing of deaths differ greatly between discourse time and story time in the novels.
claims.quote: differ greatly between discourse time and story time

claims.claim: Vale counts 24 point of view characters in the first five novels once prologue and epilogue chapters are set aside.
claims.source: Richard Vale, 'Bayesian Prediction for The Winds of Winter', arXiv:1409.5830, 2014
claims.quote: 24 characters have had chapters told from their point of view

claims.claim: Kyrchanoff argues that the authors of The World of Ice and Fire imitated the style of the medieval chronicle and synthesised it with simplified modern historical representations.
claims.source: Maksim W. Kyrchanoff, Journal of Frontier Studies 2018 no. 1
claims.quote: actually imitated the style of the medieval chronicle

claims.claim: Kyrchanoff notes the imagined chronicler of The World of Ice and Fire gives the age of the world as a range from 40 to 500 thousand years rather than a fixed figure.
claims.source: Maksim W. Kyrchanoff, Journal of Frontier Studies 2018 no. 1
claims.quote: his estimates ranged from 40 to 500 thousand years

claims.claim: The passage Kyrchanoff quotes from The World of Ice and Fire page 79 shows the chronicler correcting his own titulature in a parenthesis, noting Dorne had not submitted.
claims.source: Martin, Antonsson and Garcia, The World of Ice and Fire (2014), p. 79, as quoted by Kyrchanoff (2018)
claims.quote: was the style used, though Dorne had not submitted
claims.page: body of the article, quoting Martin, Antonsson, & Garcia, 2014, p. 79

claims.claim: Kirkus's unsigned 1996 review of A Game of Thrones calls the series title A Song of Ice and Fire insipid.
claims.source: Kirkus Reviews (unsigned), review of A Game of Thrones, 1 July 1996
claims.quote: entitled, insipidly enough, A Song of Ice and Fire

claims.claim: Kirkus's 1996 review credits A Game of Thrones with an intricate plot articulated against a backdrop of real depth and texture.
claims.source: Kirkus Reviews (unsigned), review of A Game of Thrones, 1 July 1996
claims.quote: an intricate plot flawlessly articulated against a backdrop of real depth

claims.claim: Kirkus's 1996 review describes A Game of Thrones as 672 pages and calls those pages dense.
claims.source: Kirkus Reviews (unsigned), review of A Game of Thrones, 1 July 1996

claims.claim: The 1996 Publishers Weekly review names accomplished prose as one of three qualities that make A Game of Thrones stand out from similar work.
claims.source: Publishers Weekly (unsigned starred review), A Game of Thrones, 29 July 1996
claims.quote: superbly developed characters, accomplished prose and sheer bloody-mindedness

verdicts.trueWording: That is even true for George R. R. Martin himself.
verdicts.note: Raw route: live link.springer.com served a JS 'Client Challenge' block; recovered via Wayback raw capture 20250801025545id_ of the exact URL (open-access chapter, full body present). Page: screenplay writers 'will usually lack any expert knowledge about the historical stages of English. That is even true for George R. R. Martin himself.' Quote exact; every limb supported. Metadata nit only (not a claim limb): the passage sits in section 3.2 'Archaisms and Pseudo-Archaisms', not section 4.

verdicts.trueWording: Ice and Fire is presented from the personal perspectives of 24 point of view (POV) characters.
verdicts.note: Live pnas.org returned HTTP 403; verified on TWO raw routes that both carry the full text: Wayback raw capture 20250710185328id_ of the exact URL, and PMC7682562 efetch XML. Quote exact in both. It is the first sentence of Results, as the claim's page field states.

verdicts.trueWording: Of these, we consider 14 to be major: eight or more chapters.
verdicts.note: Same two raw routes (Wayback id_ capture + PMC XML); quote exact in both. The page's full criterion reads 'eight or more chapters, mostly titled with their names, are relayed from their perspectives' - the claim quotes the chapter threshold only, but that threshold is stated as the criterion and is what excludes Arys Oakheart in the paper's own example, so no limb is unsupported.

verdicts.trueWording: From the five books containing 343 chapters, 2,007 characters were identified.
verdicts.note: Same two raw routes; quote exact in both, in Results / 'Evolution of the Social Network Structure' exactly as the page field states. Both limbs (343 chapters across five books; 2,007 characters identified) explicit.

verdicts.trueWording: of which 1,806 interact with another at least once
verdicts.note: Same two raw routes; quote exact in both, same sentence as index 678 in 'Evolution of the Social Network Structure'.

verdicts.trueWording: it is geometric rather than power law
verdicts.note: Same two raw routes; quote exact in the Abstract, which also carries the second limb verbatim: 'This provides measurable support for the widely held view that significant deaths in A Song of Ice and Fire are unpredictable chapter by chapter,' and 'intervals between significant deaths in chapters'.

verdicts.trueWording: the order and pacing of deaths differ greatly between discourse time and story time
verdicts.note: Same two raw routes; quote exact, in the discussion paragraph immediately preceding Materials and Methods. Page defines discourse time as 'the order and pacing of events as experienced by the reader'.

verdicts.trueWording: So far, ignoring prologue and epilogue chapters, 24 characters have had POV chapters.
verdicts.note: arXiv abstract page carries only the abstract, so I fetched the paper PDF (arxiv.org/pdf/1409.5830v1, 8 pp) and extracted its text. Section 1.1 reads: 'Five books have so far been published... So far, ignoring prologue and epilogue chapters in some of the books, 24 characters have had chapters told from their point of view.' Quote exact; every limb (five novels, prologue/epilogue set aside, 24) supported, in section 1.1 as stated.

verdicts.trueWording: the real authors of the text actually imitated the style of the medieval chronicle
verdicts.note: Fetched the cyberleninka PDF directly (HTTP 200, 30 pp) and extracted text. Full sentence: '...the real authors of the text actually imitated the style of the medieval chronicle, synthesized it with modern simplistic historical representations.' Quote exact; the synthesis limb is explicit ('simplified' = the page's 'simplistic').

verdicts.trueWording: the imagined author... allowed himself reasoning about the age of the world; his estimates ranged from 40 to 500 thousand years
verdicts.note: Same PDF. Quote exact. 'Rather than a fixed figure' is carried by the page's own 'estimates ranged from...to'; the chronicler is 'the imagined author of the historical chronicle'.

verdicts.trueWording: ("Seven Kingdoms" was the style used, though Dorne had not submitted. Nor would it, for more than a century to come) (Martin, Antonsson, & Garcia, 2014, p. 79)
verdicts.note: Same PDF. Quote exact, and the parenthesis, the p. 79 citation, and the Dorne limb are all on the page: the block quote proclaims Aegon 'Lord of the Seven Kingdoms' and then qualifies that style in the parenthesis. 'Correcting his own titulature' is the analyst's characterization of what the page shows as a parenthetical self-qualification of the style just used - substantively supported, not a separate assertion.

verdicts.trueWording: the first of a fantasy series entitled, insipidly enough, A Song of Ice and Fire
verdicts.note: Live kirkusreviews.com fetched with a browser UA (HTTP 200). Quote exact, in the review's opening sentence. Review carries no byline (unsigned) and the page states 'Kirkus Reviews Issue: July 1, 1996'.

verdicts.trueWording: A vast, rich saga... an intricate plot flawlessly articulated against a backdrop of real depth and texture.
verdicts.note: Same live Kirkus page. Quote exact, in the closing verdict; 'and texture' follows immediately, so the claim's 'depth and texture' limb is on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: Still, after 672 dense pages, were you expecting a satisfying resolution?
verdicts.note: Same live Kirkus page. Quote exact, and the page's metadata independently reads 'Page Count: 672'.

verdicts.trueWording: the book stands out from similar work by Eddings, Brooks and others by virtue of its superbly developed characters, accomplished prose and sheer bloody-mindedness
verdicts.note: Live publishersweekly.com fetched with a browser UA (HTTP 200). Quote exact; accomplished prose is the second of exactly three named qualities, and the 'stand out from similar work' limb is the same sentence. Page states 'Reviewed on: 07/29/1996'.
